title: Data Center & Networking Daily Briefing
description: AI fabrics and enterprise networking, data center capacity, power and cooling, and AI storage.
readFirst: Covers Nov. 3–13. New: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 12 that Yandex Cloud said 2.84 percent of customer data cannot be restored after Ukrainian drone strikes on its data centers. The Nov. 4 local ballot-measure note was dropped so the capacity subsection stayed at four items. Dell's OneFS 9.16 note remains on the partners page. A Nov. 12 Tom's Hardware headline about marijuana farms considering data-center sites was not used.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: Microsoft lobbies against an FCC ban on Chinese optical transceivers
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 10, citing Reuters, that Microsoft, which Tom's Hardware said is building 35 data centers in the United States and planning 134 more, has met with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and the National Security Council as the FCC considers an import ban on Chinese optical transceivers. Tom's Hardware said Microsoft and the Information Technology Industry Council are lobbying against the ban. John Miller, the council's executive vice president of policy and general counsel, said the move threatens to grind the data-center rollout to a halt because AI chips sit unused without transceivers to connect them. Tom's Hardware said Chinese companies supply 66 percent of the global market.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: Yandex Cloud says 2.84 percent of customer data cannot be restored
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 12 that Yandex Cloud said it had restored access to more than 97 percent of customer data after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged its data centers, and that the remaining 2.84 percent cannot be restored because of critical equipment damage. Tom's Hardware said Yandex attributed part of that loss to customers who had no backups on the platform, and that customers who used Yandex Cloud backup tools did not lose data. Tom's Hardware said it knows of at least three Yandex locations damaged in the strikes.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: SpaceX is designing a 72-GPU Rubin rack for data centers in space
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 11, citing SemiAnalysis, that SpaceX and xAI are developing a custom version of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, codenamed Kessel, for terrestrial and orbital data centers. Tom's Hardware said the design keeps 36 Vera CPUs, 72 Rubin GPUs, and nine NVLink switch trays, and replaces internal NVLink cable cartridges with compute and switch trays set back-to-back around a passive printed-circuit midplane. It said that midplane is an 84-layer board using M10 copper-clad laminates, compared with the 156-layer M9 backplane SemiAnalysis described for Nvidia's Kyber design. Tom's Hardware said SpaceX and xAI would still buy Nvidia hardware from Nvidia and source other components independently.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: data-center fiber demand is pricing out Ukraine's tethered drones
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 11 that a BlueBird Tech research-and-development representative told Ars Technica that fiber-optic cable prices have risen about six to 10 times in the past couple of years as AI data-center demand takes more of the supply. Tom's Hardware said the interview estimated that Ukraine and Russia produce about 50,000 fiber-optic drones a month, with ranges up to 62 miles. It said Ukraine acquired 72 miles of fiber from Chinese suppliers in August 2025, while Russia imported 328,000 miles that month, and that Russia acquired 37 million miles in all of 2025, over 10 percent of global production. Tom's Hardware said the same account estimated a 111-million-mile global shortfall, and that the BlueBird representative claimed some Chinese companies have refused to sell fiber to Ukraine.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: Dutch police arrested protesters at a Microsoft data-center site in Amsterdam
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 6 that about a hundred protesters entered a Microsoft data center under construction in Amsterdam, which Pure Data Centers owns, and that the Stop Dirty Data Centers coalition said it was planning actions across 16 countries on Nov. 6 and 7, with a map showing 85 locations. Pure Data Centers asked people on site to leave and talk, and Microsoft said it respected peaceful expression and does not condone unlawful action. Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 8 that Amsterdam police arrested 150 to 200 protesters at the site on suspicion of trespassing after some entered the construction site with violence, and that police seized break-in tools. It said the Dutch outlet NOS identified the group at the site that day as Fossielvrij.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: SoftBank takes a $3.7 billion hit canceling 13 gigawatts of turbines
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 11, citing The Wall Street Journal, that SoftBank is taking a $3.7 billion earnings hit after canceling reservations for gas turbines it had booked to power AI data centers. Tom's Hardware said the Journal, citing people familiar with the orders, reported SoftBank had reserved more than 13 gigawatts of turbines. It said the news followed a denial by SoftBank's chief financial officer of Elon Musk's claim that the company had defaulted on turbine-blade contracts; the officer said there is no such default. Tom's Hardware also said SoftBank plans a 9.2-gigawatt plant in Ohio, scheduled to start construction in early 2027 at a cost of $33 billion, to serve a neighboring 8-gigawatt data center that would be leased to OpenAI, and that Nvidia has discussed guaranteeing about $250 billion of financing for that project.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: Anthropic takes over $3.4 billion in Caterpillar generator orders
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 9, citing Reuters, that Anthropic agreed to spend $3.4 billion securing 1.7 gigawatts of gas-fired generators for its AI data centers by taking over equipment orders that Texas supplier OnePWR Solutions had placed with Caterpillar. Tom's Hardware said the agreement was reached in late September, includes engineering and construction to install the equipment, and that Anthropic is not buying OnePWR. It said the orders were placed about two years ago and needed more financing, and that average U.S. delivery times for large gas turbines and generators have reached six years. Tom's Hardware said taking over the existing orders lets Anthropic avoid waiting for a new slot in Caterpillar's schedule.

items.headline: NVIDIA says one Vera CPU beats the fastest and the most efficient x86 CPU it measured
items.summary: NVIDIA said Nov. 5 that, in a 100-megawatt data-center comparison, a single Vera CPU performs better than both the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. NVIDIA said Vera delivers 1.6 times more agents per watt than the fastest x86 CPU at what it called industry-leading agent speed, and twice the agent speed of the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. NVIDIA said Perplexity ran agentic coding tasks 1.5 times faster on Vera than on traditional CPUs and plans to deploy Vera in a production system, and that Daytona brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds on Vera versus 88.4 seconds on x86. NVIDIA said the comparison is about running more agents inside a power limit, because agent steps move between GPU reasoning and CPU execution.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: xAI is powering a Mississippi data center with eight jet turbines
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 3 that Elon Musk's xAI is using eight converted jet-engine turbines to power a Mississippi data center. Tom's Hardware said the generators have state-level permission, and that the permits allow a 25 percent higher limit for volatile organic compounds. It said those compounds, together with carbon monoxide, have drawn warnings from environmentalists, and that The New York Times reports the Southern Environmental Law Center has challenged Mississippi's decision to approve the turbines.

items.headline: Tom's Hardware: a smuggler says banned HBM is reaching China inside cheap processors
items.summary: Tom's Hardware reported Nov. 3, citing The Information, that a memory smuggler described moving export-controlled high-bandwidth memory from South Korea into China. Tom's Hardware said the person owns a chip-design firm that builds cheap, low-performing processors covered by U.S. and South Korean export controls, then pairs them with high-bandwidth memory from Samsung and SK hynix that would be banned on its own. It said the export rules, as Tom's Hardware describes them, look at the server processor's performance and not at the other components attached to it.
